title: CHAPTER ELEVEN. On the distribution of sacred theology
english:
CHAPTER ELEVEN
On the distribution of sacred theology
So far we have seen the definition, nature, and principles of sacred theology.
The parts follow, of which there are two: the common and the proper.

Since sacred theology is a practical discipline of its own kind, as was shown above in chapter 1, section 3, it is to be treated, by the common judgment even of the philosophers who are masters of the best order, in the analytic order.

According to that order both the whole doctrine itself and all its parts will be treated from its chief end, and each head will occupy the place that suits it by its primary relation to its own whole and to the end of the whole

title: II. Various tractations; Conrad Bergius's five modes — history and prophecy
english: II. Among outstanding theologians there are various treatments and divisions of it.
Doctor Conrad Bergius, in his praised Precognita, refers the tractations of sacred things to five modes.
The first is HISTORY, which is discourse about singular past deeds; in it the order of time is chiefly to be observed.

The second is PROPHECY, which is discourse about singular future deeds; in it partly the order of time is observed, partly the prudence or fitness to the particular end that God or the prophet intends.

title: Invocation and exhortation (precept, persuasion, congratulation)
english: The third is INVOCATION, which is discourse either proclaiming God's past benefits or asking for future ones; and it uses the order that affection, place, and time nearly dictate.
The fourth is EXHORTATION, which is discourse not so much declaring some deed done or to come as wanting and requiring something to be done by a human being.

It includes (1) a precept about doing or omitting; (2) persuasion, which works by promising and threatening, or by foretelling the goods the obedient will obtain and the evils the resistant will run into; (3) congratulation, complaint, consolation, and the like, which call for joy or patience or sorrow by praising present goods and lessening or enlarging evils, and so on.
And this mode of sacred speech again uses chiefly the order of prudence, or fitness to the affection that is to be stirred or calmed in the hearer.

title: Didascalia: positive, free, particular, universal, catechetical, systematic
english: The fifth is DIDASCALIA properly so called, which is either bound to the text it interprets — and from that text its order chiefly depends — whence it is called positive theology, because by interpreting Scripture it lays down the principles and foundations of theological dogmas;

or it is free, and that particular, about a certain argument only: if it is taught in a popular manner, it is fitted to the time, place, and capacity of the hearers; if by the rule of art or scholastically, it nearly follows the laws of treating a theme logically;
or it is universal, and that either compendious or catechetical about all or at least most things necessary to salvation, or full or systematic about all or most things revealed from heaven.
And this can be twofold: historical and logical.

title: The historical method of didascalia; the text of Scripture
english: 1. The HISTORICAL is that which narrates in order what has been given, commanded, and done by God and by human beings.
It inserts prophecies, prayers, and exhortations partly into the narration itself, as the order of events allows, and partly sets them apart like certain special acts and documents of the kingdom.

This method is not only popular but also especially fitting to the nature of the subject, which is the kingdom — and a certain and singular one — by which God chiefly governs this world and the Church.

It has therefore been used in the sacred letters, useful and necessary for the learned and the unlearned, for whom no study ought to be preferred to grasping the TEXT OF SCRIPTURE with understanding and memory as far as can be done (Second Timothy 3:15; First Timothy 4:10).

title: The logical method; two ways of arranging; differences from subjects, objects, ends
english: 2. The LOGICAL is that which aptly distinguishes the parts of the divine kingdom and their acts recalled to certain genera, and brings together under one head the parallels that occur scattered in the Scriptures, so that the joining of both methods may give greater light and help to understanding and memory alike.
It can be instituted in two ways.

First, when the end of the doctrine is known beforehand and the subject is set, the acts that are certain means to the end are enumerated nearly in the order in which they follow one another — the method we most approve in compendia and summaries of Christian doctrine, and which we follow in this handbook and idea of theology.

Second, the acts of God's kingdom can be so enumerated and divided that differences are taken chiefly from the subjects or matter of the kingdom; for habits and acts are specified chiefly by subjects and ends, as we taught in chapter 1, section 7.

Remote differences are taken from acting subjects (for example common-place classes about the acts of God and of man, and specifically about the acts and offices of pastors, parents, children, magistrates, subjects, and so on); nearer differences in the acts of each subject are taken from the objects toward which the action tends (for example man's acts and offices toward God, himself, neighbor, friends, enemies, the poor, the rich, and so on); nearest differences are taken from the end or good the action intends and introduces from subject into subject (for example man's acts and offices toward the neighbor as to the good of intellect, will, body, outward worship, and so on).

title: Memory and intellect served by the method; DIVISIONES of theology 1–5
english: A method of this kind most agrees with a full syntagma of common places, and is most useful to memory and understanding (which alone is to be looked to in method).
To memory, because when a few elements — subjects, objects, ends — are known, from their varied combination as of letters one may see and number in order many classes of acts as of words.

To understanding, because this method will keep more exactly and set out more clearly the analogy of the Church, household, and commonwealth of God, of father and prince; of the Christian as son and subject; of pastor, steward, legate, and the like.
The DIVISIONS of theology vary no less.
1. Some divide into doctrine concerning God and concerning God's actions or works.
2. Others, with doctrine of principles, end, and efficient cause first set down, divide into the methodological and the therapeutic.
3. Others, with principles first — the Word of God and God himself — set as parts the causes of our salvation, and so God's works and effects, and its subject, namely man.
4. Others divide into the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
5. Others into doctrine concerning God and the Church.

title: Divisiones 6–10; Polanus on faith and good works
english: 6. Others divide concerning God and the motion of the rational creature toward God.
7. Others into doctrine concerning God, concerning creatures and especially concerning man and his fall, concerning restoration through Christ, and concerning the sacraments and the life to come.

8. Others into doctrine concerning faith and good works, as Doctor Amandus Polanus does in his Syntagma Theologiae, book 2, chapter 1, where he gives the reasons for that division and confirms it by the authority of older doctors — Ignatius, Irenaeus, Lactantius, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, the Council of Toledo, and the Historia Tripartita — and of more recent ones: the Helvetic Confession, Theodore Beza, the Irenaeus of our age, Lambert Daneau, Zanchi, Ursinus, and Kinedoncius.
9. Others concerning God the testator, Christ the mediator, and the Church the heir.
10. Others finally distribute into theory concerning God, sin, and Christ, and into conversion and its fruits.

title: III. Analytic distribution into the common and proper parts
english: III. All treatises and partitions by which the body of sacred theology is explained easily please us, provided that at least in the chief foundations of faith and salvation they agree with Sacred Scripture.

And without taking anything from anyone, we gladly and with thanksgiving give each theologian his due praise; yet with the good leave of others whose gifts we admire and revere, for easier knowledge and practice, as we set out to sketch theology as a practical discipline, we will now follow the analytic order and not inconveniently distribute it into the TWO aforesaid PARTS, the COMMON and the PROPER.
We do so because theological dogmas stand in a twofold difference.

Some contain those acts of God's kingdom that somehow belong to all who desire to be saved — namely the chief heads of the Christian religion as articles of faith and foundations of our salvation, which no one may ignore — and their interpretations, illustrations, religious determinations, and conclusions formed jointly from Scripture's dictates as theological principles by a disciplinary method and order mixed together and treated scholastically for the use of learned youth; once rightly known, these are not to be denied or attacked but approved and received and practiced by anyone according to the measure of his grace and age.

Others embrace those acts that belong not to all but chiefly to those who ought to save themselves and others and who hold ecclesiastical office first of all, or scholastic, political, or economic office, or are at least some part of such orders, whether they preside over others or are under them.

The former we will treat under the common part, the latter under the proper part, with the help of God Most High, mindful as to manner of treatment of that Augustinian precept that theology rather requires foundations than ornaments, and as to the matter itself of that saying of Ambrose or Prosper or Eucherius in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 7: What God willed to be hidden is not to be searched out; what he has made plain is not to be denied — lest in the former we be found unlawfully curious, and in the latter damnably ungrateful.

title: Liber I corona: six requirements of the theology student; theodidaktos close
english: And so that I may seal this first book of our theology with some closing mark, I will here show under the image of a well-born disciple the divine craft and the short way by which the sacred scriptures, as the tables of the Christian kingdom and the roots of true theology, may be read with fruit.

Six things especially are required in a disciple who is to advance far and happily by great daily journeys: (1) age, (2) talent, (3) a faithful teacher, (4) study and labor faithfully to be devoted to the instructor, (5) continual exercise by which he can recite the lesson exactly when the teacher demands it, (6) reverence toward the instructor.
The same things are asked of the student of sacred theology who desires to turn the sacred letters and God's Word to the good of his own soul.
For (1) let him have a firm resolve to put off the old man, that in Christ he may become a new man, indeed a man of God, for whom Sacred Scripture is uniquely destined (Second Timothy 3:16–17).
(2) From God our LORD let him humbly ask with earnest and frequent groans for spiritual understanding and spiritual judgment (James 1:5; Luke 11:9–13).
(3) To JESUS CHRIST, the Master whose chair is in the heavens, let him look with unturned eyes and rightly acknowledge him.
(4) In this divine school let him be assiduous, and not only read but reread what he has read, and with eyes and heart lifted together to heaven meditate and ruminate on what he reads.

(5) Let him weigh one reading against another, render it to the heavenly Master, seek the foundation of truth in him alone, practice by day and by night the doctrine received from him, often remember it, and anxiously ask that he himself may daily become better from himself.

(6) Let him endure under the discipline and correction of Christ and of his Spirit, the heavenly teacher; let him revere and love him, and in his studies seek nothing outside God's glory and his own soul's salvation.
Such a one in Sacred Scripture and theology, or the mysteries of God's kingdom, as θεοδίδακτος — taught by God — will advance most excellently and be blessed forever in heaven.

For this is properly necessary: that whoever desires to understand the sacred letters inwardly and savingly, still more to interpret them for others and apply them with fruit, must first repent, revere God, be willing to acknowledge Christ in his kingdom according to the Spirit and to press his footsteps in the crowd of this world, and ardently ask the spirit of faith and of divine wisdom from him who opened his disciples' mind that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:46).
